title: God, Nature, and Right Action
body:
God, Nature, and Right Action

Having explained the indestructible nature of the soul, Sree Krishna turns to the laws governing nature (Prakriti) and the mechanism of human action (Karma). The physical universe, with all its sensory elements, is the ever-changing, inferior energy of the Divine. Behind it stands the supreme Paramaathma, whose will holds together all universal changes.

ममैवांशो जीवलोके जीवभूतः सनातनः ।
मनःषष्ठानीन्द्रियाणि प्रकृतिस्थानि कर्षति ।।

"The embodied souls in this material world are My eternal fragmental parts. But bound by material nature, they are struggling with the six senses, including the mind."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XV, Verse 7

शरीरं यदवाप्नोति यच्चाप्युत्क्रामतीश्वरः ।
गृहीत्वैतानि संयाति वायुर्गन्धानिवाशयात् ।।

"As the air carries fragrance from place to place, so does the embodied soul carry the mind and senses with it when it leaves an old body and enters a new one."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XV, Verse 8

श्रोत्रं चक्षुः स्पर्शनं च रसनं घ्राणमेव च ।
अधिष्ठाय मनश्चायं विषयानुपसेवते ।।

"Using the sense perceptions of the ears, eyes, skin, tongue, and nose, which are grouped around the mind, the embodied soul savours the objects of the senses."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XV, Verse 9

At death, when the soul departs, it carries with it the cumulative impressions of its activities like air carrying fragrance. This collection of tendencies (Samskaras) determines its next physical receptacle. However, the soul is bound only when it seeks to be the 'doer' and desires the fruits of its actions.

इति क्षेत्रं तथा ज्ञानं ज्ञेयं चोक्तं समासतः ।
मद्भक्त एतद्विज्ञाय मद्भावायोपपद्यते ।।

"I have thus revealed to you the nature of the field, the meaning of knowledge, and the object of knowledge. Only My devotees can understand this in reality, and by doing so, they attain My divine nature."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XIII, Verse 20

कार्यकारणकर्तृत्वे हेतुः प्रकृतिरुच्यते ।
पुरुषः सुखदुःखानां भोक्तृत्वे हेतुरुच्यते ।।

"In the matter of creation, the material energy is responsible for cause and effect; in the matter of experiencing happiness and distress, the individual soul is declared responsible."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XIII, Verse 21

पुरुषः प्रकृतिस्थो हि भुङ्क्ते प्रकृतिजान्गुणान् ।
कारणं गुणसङ्गोऽस्य सदसद्योनिजन्मसु ।।

"When the purusha (individual soul) seated in prakriti (the material energy) desires to enjoy the three gunas, attachment to them becomes the cause of its birth in superior and inferior wombs."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter XIII, Verse 22

To escape this cycle of birth and death, the Lord reveals the supreme doctrine of Nishkama Karma—performing one's prescribed worldly duties with complete dedication, but with absolute detachment from the results. Action must not be abandoned; rather, selfish desire must be surrendered.

कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन ।
मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि ।।

"You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions. Never consider yourself to be the cause of the results of your activities, nor be attached to inaction."
— Bhagavad Gita, Chapter II, Verse 47

★ THE ESSENCE OF NISHKAMA KARMA ★
Sree Krishna asserts that the activities of the world must continue to maintain cosmic and social order (Lokasangraha). A wise seeker performs his tasks as a consecrated offering to the Divine, recognizing that the natural modes of energy (Gunas) are the actual doers, while the true inner self remains a silent, untainted witness.
